class: ONE PAGE, TWO CANDIDATES OF THE SAME CLASS, OPPOSITE VERDICTS. Both were one-letter differences on real words in a lemma, both were flagged by the translating agent as [var:] against the Clementine, and both were named as plate-read candidates. The plate splits them: 0743C *lignis* is OURS (Migne prints *ignis*, so there is no divergence at all and the marker is withdrawn), while 0744C *vide* is MIGNE'S (he prints the imperative where the Clementine has *vidi*, and his own gloss re-quotes *vidi* three times four lines below). ⭐ This is the argument for the plate in one page: corpus frequency and Vulgate collation cannot tell these two apart, because they look identical from the file. Only the plate does. || SECOND READ, p. 372: the 0733B `[cj:]` dissolved — Migne prints *infructuosos* hyphenated across a line break and the digitization failed to rejoin it. Raised by the blind polarity reader as an observation, not as a finding; it was right that the conjecture sat oddly, and the plate showed why.

patches.why: THE PLATE PRINTS *ignis*. PL 114 p. 377, col. 743, VERS. 12: 'Sicut flamma ignis.' Corpus Corporum inserted an l, manufacturing a word (a flame OF TIMBER for a flame OF FIRE). Our Latin column was therefore printing a word Migne did not print, and the English carried a [var:] asserting a divergence from Apc 19:12 that does not exist — a public claim about another text, resting on our own digitization's error. Restoring *ignis* removes both. The gloss that follows (*Quia comburit vitia, et accendit, et illuminat* — it burns, kindles, enlightens) is about FIRE and never mentions wood, which is the corroboration from inside the work.

patches.why: THE LINE-BREAK REJOIN, IN MIRROR IMAGE OF 8946 *Salomomonis*. PL 114 p. 372, col. 733, VERS. 18 prints the word hyphenated across the line break — *in-* at the end of one line, *fructuosos* at the head of the next — and Corpus Corporum FAILED TO REJOIN IT, leaving two words where Migne has one. (At 8946 the same digitization rejoined a hyphenated word and duplicated the syllable; here it did the opposite.) Our column anchor then landed in the gap, producing `in [0733B] fructuosos`, which read as the positive *fructuosos* and forced a `[cj:]` conjecturing the privative. ⭐ THERE WAS NEVER ANYTHING TO CONJECTURE: Migne prints *infructuosos*. The conjecture was correct in substance — *super arenam* requires the unfruitful — and it was wholly unnecessary. The marker is withdrawn and the word made whole, with the anchor kept at the line break where Migne's band B falls. ⚑ Corroborated from the source side exactly as 8946 was: the TEI preserves a newline on BOTH sides of the <pb/>, which is where the printed hyphen and the line turn stand. ⚑ THE GENERAL LESSON: an anchor that appears to fall INSIDE a word is a rejoin candidate before it is a conjecture candidate — check the plate for a hyphen before reaching for [cj:].

refuted.candidate: *Et vide sedes* — flagged as possibly our corruption of *vidi*
refuted.verdict: NOT ours. THE PLATE PRINTS *vide*, the imperative, exactly as our text has it: PL 114 p. 377, col. 744, 'VERS. 4. — Et vide sedes.' The Clementine has *Et vidi sedes*, so the [var:] is CONFIRMED and stands. Migne's own gloss immediately below reads 'Ligato diabolo, VIDI solutos fideles ... VIDI in tempore ligationis ... vidi statim in gloriam intrare' — the plate contradicts its own lemma three times over, which is precisely what this edition exists to show. Recorded so the marker is not re-questioned.
